sections.sectionSummaryBrief: Rosh Chodesh Sivan is the preparation for receiving the Torah, symbolized by the new moon's point of bittul (self-nullification), which reflects the bittul inherent in every Jew.

translations.translation: And this is, "In the third month... on this day they came to the wilderness of Sinai,"
that on Rosh Chodesh Sivan was the preparation for receiving the Torah,
because on Rosh Chodesh is the birth of the moon,
when then
(at the time of the birth)
it is only a single point,
and this indicates its bittul (self-nullification),
that it has nothing of itself at all.
And so it is with Israel, who are similar and count by the moon,
that on Rosh Chodesh is a time fit for revealing the power of bittul that exists in each one of Israel.
Therefore on Rosh Chodesh Sivan is the preparation for receiving the Torah,
that a person's study of Torah should be with bittul,
like one who answers after the one who calls out.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: Rosh Chodesh Sivan is the preparation for receiving the Torah because the counting of the Omer, corresponding to the seven sefiros, culminates with the completion of the primary sefiros in the sefirah of Malchus.

translations.translation: And the maamar continues with further explanation of this, that Rosh Chodesh Sivan is the preparation for receiving the Torah,
for when Israel left Egypt they began to count the Omer,
which is the preparation for receiving the Torah,
and the seven weeks of the counting of the Omer
("Seven weeks you shall count for yourself")
correspond to the seven sefiros (midos),
and on Rosh Chodesh Sivan, which is the third day of the seventh week, there already exist the three sefiros of Chesed, Gevurah, and Tiferes
(which are the primary sefiros)
of the counting of Malchus,
and it is as if the entire seventh week already exists,
and therefore on Rosh Chodesh Sivan they came to the wilderness of Sinai, because then the main preparation for the Giving of the Torah was completed.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: The maamar explains two aspects of preparation for receiving the Torah—the perfection of the person and his bittul—both of which are present on Rosh Chodesh Sivan through the moon's bittul and the completion of the sefiros via the Omer.

translations.translation: And it can be said,
that which the maamar explains two explanations regarding this, that Rosh Chodesh Sivan is the preparation for receiving the Torah,
is,
because in the preparation for receiving the Torah there are two matters.
The perfection of the person,
that in order for him to be fit to receive the Torah, he must be at the ultimate level of perfection.
And his bittul (self-nullification).
For since the Torah is infinitely higher than the person
(all the more so than it is higher than the upper worlds),
therefore,
when the person has a sense of self-existence,
his existence is
(like)
the opposite of the Torah,
and in order for the person to receive the Torah, it is through his bittul.
And therefore the maamar explains,
that this—that on Rosh Chodesh Sivan they came to the wilderness of Sinai and were prepared to receive the Torah—
is,
because on Rosh Chodesh Sivan there exist both matters.
This, that on Rosh Chodesh is the birth of the moon,
when then it is only a single point,
bittul.
And this, that on Rosh Chodesh Sivan the primary sefiros were completed
(also)
in the counting of Malchus—the perfection of the person.
And two matters in the perfection of the person that is accomplished through the counting of the Omer.
That the counting of the Omer is the matter of refining and purifying the midos (attributes),
and that through the counting of the Omer there is the drawing down of the forty-nine gates of Binah (understanding).
